mcqs.why: The correct answer is 65°. Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so each one is 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, one angle is 65°. What is each consecutive angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 115°. Consecutive angles in a parallelogram are supplementary, so each is 180° − 65° = 115°.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram WXYZ, ∠X is double ∠W, and they are consecutive angles. What is ∠W?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 60°. ∠X + ∠W = 180° and ∠X = 2∠W, so 3∠W = 180° and ∠W = 60°.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, diagonal AC is double diagonal BD and AC + BD = 9 cm. What is AC?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 6 cm. If BD = d then AC = 2d, so 3d = 9, d = 3, and AC = 2 × 3 = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: The diagonals of parallelogram ABCD meet at P. AC = 6 cm and BD = 3 cm. What is PA?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3 cm. The diagonals bisect each other, so PA is half of AC: PA = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.

mcqs.q: With PA = 3 cm and PB = 1.5 cm, what is mPA : mPB in simplest form?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2 : 1. Divide both parts of 3 : 1.5 by 1.5 to get the simplest ratio 2 : 1.

mcqs.q: What is a chord of a circle?
options: A line that touches the circle at one point
A line that cuts the circle at two points
The line segment joining two points of a circle
The part bounded by two radii and an arc
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the line segment joining two points of a circle. That is the book's definition of a chord.

mcqs.q: What is a secant of a circle?
options: The line that cuts a circle at two points
The line that touches the circle at exactly one point
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the line that cuts a circle at two points. That is the book's definition of a secant.

mcqs.q: What is a sector of a circle?
options: The line segment joining two points of a circle
A line touching the circle at one point
The part of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the part of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc. That is the book's definition of a sector.

mcqs.q: What is a tangent line to a circle?
options: A line that cuts the circle at two points
The line that touches the circle at exactly one point
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the line that touches the circle at exactly one point. That is the book's definition of a tangent line.

mcqs.q: A circle has radius 3 cm. Point Q is 2.5 cm from the centre O. Where is Q?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is inside the circle. Q's distance 2.5 cm is less than the radius 3 cm, so Q lies inside the circle.

mcqs.q: A circle has radius 3 cm. Point R is 4 cm from the centre O. Where is R?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is outside the circle. R's distance 4 cm is greater than the radius 3 cm, so R lies outside the circle.

mcqs.q: What are concentric circles?
options: Points that lie on the same circle
Circles with the same centre but different radii
Circles with different centres and the same radius
mcqs.why: The correct answer is circles with the same centre but different radii. That is the book's definition of concentric circles.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 7
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

Parallel lines are lines that lie in the same plane and never meet. Two lines which are parallel to the same line are also parallel to each other. A polygon is a closed figure consisting of three or more than three sides, and a polygon whose all sides are equal is called a regular polygon.

A circle is the set of points which are at an equal distance from a fixed point, that is, the centre. An arc is a part of the circumference of a circle, that is, the part between two points on the circle.

TermDefinition given in the book
Parallel linesLines that lie in the same plane and never meet
ParallelogramA quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel; in the fill-in work, whose opposite sides are parallel and equal
ArcA part of the circumference of a circle, the part between two points on the circle
SecantThe line that cuts a circle at two points
Tangent lineThe line that touches the circle at exactly one point
Concyclic pointsPoints that lie on the same circle
Concentric circlesCircles with the same centre but different radii
ChordA line segment which joins two points of a circle

Rules

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, pairs of corresponding angles are equal.

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, pairs of alternate angles are equal.

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, pairs of same-side interior angles are supplementary.

The quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram.

In a parallelogram, the same-side (consecutive) angles are supplementary.

In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal and opposite sides are equal.

A line which passes through the midpoint of one side of a triangle and is parallel to the second side bisects the third side.

Sum of interior angles of a polygon: S = (2n − 4) right angles, that is, (2n − 4) × 90°.

Diameter = 2 × radius, and radius = diameter ÷ 2.

Exactly one circle can pass through three non-collinear points.

Worked Example

Example: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.

Step 1: A regular octagon is a closed figure with all eight sides equal and all eight angles equal.

Step 2: So the number of sides is n = 8.

Step 3: Use the sum formula S = (2n − 4) × 90°.

Step 4: Put n = 8: 2n = 16.

Step 5: Then 2n − 4 = 16 − 4 = 12.

Step 6: So S = 12 × 90° = 1080°.

Step 7: All eight angles are equal, so divide the sum by 8.

Step 8: Each interior angle = 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°.

Remember

  • Fill-in facts: parallel lines lie in the same plane and never meet; a parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal; its consecutive angles are supplementary.
  • In parallelogram PQRS with m∠P = 70°, mPS = 3 cm and mRS = 4 cm: ∠R = 70°, ∠Q = ∠S = 110°, PQ = 4 cm and QR = 3 cm.
  • Making the sides of a parallelogram 1 1/2 times bigger does not change its angles, so m∠A = m∠P = 70°, not 3/2 × 70°.
  • With side AD extended to E and m∠CDE = 65°: ∠ADC = 115°, ∠ABC = 115°, ∠DAB = 65° and ∠BCD = 65°.
  • Regular pentagon: sum 540°, each angle 108°. Regular hexagon: sum 720°, each angle 120°. Regular octagon: sum 1080°, each angle 135°.
  • Three concentric circles with diameters 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm have radii 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 5 cm.
  • Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points, and exactly one circle passes through four concyclic points.

mcqs.q: Two lines which lie in the same plane and never meet are called what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is parallel lines. By the book's definition, lines in the same plane that never meet are parallel.

mcqs.q: Two lines are each parallel to the same line. What is true about the two lines?
options: They are perpendicular to each other
They are also parallel to each other
They are the same line only
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they are also parallel to each other. Two lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.

mcqs.q: A polygon is a closed figure consisting of how many sides?
options: Three or more than three sides
mcqs.why: The correct answer is three or more than three sides. That is the book's completed definition of a polygon.

mcqs.q: The quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a parallelogram. The book states that the quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram.

mcqs.q: What is each interior angle of a regular pentagon?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 108°. The sum is (10 − 4) × 90° = 540°, and 540° ÷ 5 = 108° for each angle.

mcqs.q: What is each interior angle of a regular hexagon?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 120°. The sum is (12 − 4) × 90° = 720°, and 720° ÷ 6 = 120° for each angle.

mcqs.q: What is each interior angle of a regular octagon?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 135°. The sum is (16 − 4) × 90° = 1080°, and 1080° ÷ 8 = 135° for each angle.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram PQRS, m∠P = 70°. What is m∠R, the opposite angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 70°. Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so ∠R = ∠P = 70°.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram PQRS, m∠P = 70°. What is m∠Q, a consecutive angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 110°. Consecutive angles are supplementary, so ∠Q = 180° − 70° = 110°.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram ABCD has sides 1 1/2 times the corresponding sides of PQRS, where m∠P = 70°. What is m∠A?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 70°. Making the sides bigger does not change the angles, so ∠A = ∠P = 70°, not 3/2 × 70°.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, side AD is extended to E and m∠CDE = 65°. What is m∠ADC?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 115°. ∠ADC and ∠CDE are neighbouring angles on a straight line, so ∠ADC = 180° − 65° = 115°.

mcqs.q: In the same figure, m∠CDE = 65° and m∠ADC = 115°. What is m∠DAB?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 65°. ∠DAB is consecutive to ∠ADC, so ∠DAB = 180° − 115° = 65°, also equal to ∠CDE by corresponding angles.

mcqs.q: A circle has a radius of 4 cm. What is the length of its diameter?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 8 cm. Diameter is double the radius, so diameter = 2 × 4 = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: Three concentric circles have diameters 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm. What is the radius of the largest circle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 5 cm. Radius is diameter divided by 2, so the largest radius is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.

mcqs.q: How many circles can pass through three non-collinear points?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is exactly one. The book states that exactly one circle can pass through three non-collinear points.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.1
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

Practical geometry means drawing exact figures with instruments — a ruler, a compass, a protractor and set squares. In this exercise we estimate angles, and construct squares, rectangles, rhombuses, parallelograms, kites, a regular pentagon and a regular hexagon from given data.

Two lines that would meet if extended are called converging lines. To find the angle between converging lines without extending them, draw any transversal cutting the two lines and subtract the sum of the two same-side angles from 180°. In the printed figures of Question 1, each meeting angle is estimated at about 25°, and measuring with a protractor also gives about 25°.

Most quadrilateral constructions use two ideas again and again: a perpendicular at a point gives a 90° angle, and the perpendicular bisector of a diagonal gives points equally distant from its ends — which is why the diagonals of a square and a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.

Steps of Construction — Square from a Diagonal (for example, diagonal AC = 6 cm)

  1. Draw the diagonal segment AC = 6 cm.
  2. Draw the perpendicular bisector of AC, cutting AC at its midpoint P.
  3. With centre P and radius PA = 3 cm, draw arcs cutting the perpendicular bisector at B and D.
  4. Join AB, BC, CD and DA.

For a diagonal of 8 cm, use the same steps with radius PA = 4 cm.

Steps of Construction — Square from a Side (for example, side BC = 7 cm)

  1. Draw side BC = 7 cm.
  2. Draw perpendiculars at B and C.
  3. With centres B and C and radius 7 cm, draw arcs cutting the perpendiculars at A and D.
  4. Join AB, CD and DA.

The same method is used for any given side, for example 2.5 cm, 3 cm, 3.5 cm, 4.5 cm, 10 cm, 11 cm or 12 cm: draw the side, raise perpendiculars at its ends, cut arcs equal to the side, and join.

Steps of Construction — Rectangle from Two Sides (for example, PQ = 6 cm, QR = 4 cm)

  1. Draw side PQ = 6 cm.
  2. Draw perpendiculars at P and Q.
  3. With centres P and Q and radius 4 cm, draw arcs cutting the perpendiculars at S and R.
  4. Join PS, SR and RQ.

Steps of Construction — Rectangle from a Side and a Diagonal (for example, AB = 4 cm, diagonal AC = 6 cm)

  1. Draw side AB = 4 cm.
  2. Draw a perpendicular at B.
  3. With centre A and radius 6 cm, draw an arc cutting the perpendicular at C.
  4. Draw a perpendicular at C and, with centre A and radius equal to BC, draw an arc cutting it at D.
  5. Join AD and DC.

Steps of Construction — Rhombus from a Side and an Angle (for example, side = 4 cm, angle A = 120°)

  1. Draw AB = 4 cm.
  2. Make a 120° angle at A and cut AD = 4 cm on its arm.
  3. With centres B and D and radius 4 cm, draw arcs meeting at C.
  4. Join BC and DC.

Steps of Construction — Rhombus from a Side and a Diagonal (for example, side PQ = 5 cm, diagonal QS = 4 cm)

  1. Draw diagonal QS = 4 cm.
  2. Draw the perpendicular bisector of QS, cutting QS at its midpoint O.
  3. With centres Q and S and radius 5 cm, draw arcs cutting the perpendicular bisector at P and R.
  4. Join PQ, QR, RS and SP.

Steps of Construction — Parallelogram from Two Diagonals and the Angle Between Them (for example, PR = 6 cm, QS = 8 cm, angle QOR = 120°)

  1. Cross the two diagonals at their midpoint O at a 120° angle, so that OP = OR = 3 cm and OQ = OS = 4 cm.
  2. Join P, Q, R and S in order.

This works because the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so each diagonal is cut into two equal halves at O.

Steps of Construction — Parallelogram from Two Adjacent Sides and the Included Angle (for example, AB = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm, angle B = 70°)

  1. Draw AB = 6 cm.
  2. Make a 70° angle at B and cut BC = 4 cm on its arm.
  3. With centres A and C and radii equal to BC and AB respectively, draw arcs meeting at D.
  4. Join AD and DC.

Steps of Construction — Kite from a Diagonal and the Two Pairs of Equal Sides (for example, diagonal BD = 4 cm, AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm)

  1. Draw diagonal BD = 4 cm.
  2. With centres B and D and radius 4 cm, draw arcs meeting at A.
  3. With centres B and D and radius 6 cm, draw arcs meeting at C, on the opposite side from A.
  4. Join AB, BC, CD and DA.

In a kite the two vertices A and C lie on opposite sides of the diagonal BD, and the diagonals cut each other perpendicularly.

Steps of Construction — Regular Pentagon from a Side (for example, side = 3.5 cm)

  1. Draw AB = 3.5 cm.
  2. Make interior angles of 108° at A and B. Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is (2 x 5 - 4) x 90° / 5 = 108°.
  3. Cut AE = BC = 3.5 cm on those arms.
  4. With centres E and C and radius 3.5 cm, draw arcs meeting at D.
  5. Join ED and DC.

The same method is used for sides of 4 cm, 4.5 cm and 5 cm.

Steps of Construction — Regular Hexagon from a Side (for example, side = 3 cm)

  1. Take centre O and draw a circle of radius 3 cm. In a regular hexagon the circumradius equals the side.
  2. Take any point A on the circle and, with the same radius of 3 cm, mark off arcs on the circle to get B, C, D, E and F.
  3. Join AB, BC, CD, DE, EF and FA.

The same method is used for sides of 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 4 cm.

Remember

  • Instruments needed: ruler, compass, protractor and set squares.
  • Square from a side: all sides are equal and all angles are 90°; check this after construction.
  • Square from a diagonal: side = diagonal / √2, so a 6 cm diagonal gives a side of about 4.24 cm and an 8 cm diagonal gives about 5.66 cm.
  • Rectangle check: diagonal = √(length² + width²), so for 6 cm and 4 cm it is √52, about 7.21 cm.
  • Rhombus: all four sides are equal; opposite angles are equal, for example with angle A = 120°, angles B and D are 60° and angle C is 120°.
  • Parallelogram: diagonals bisect each other, so work with their halves at the midpoint O.
  • Regular pentagon: each interior angle is 108°. Regular hexagon: each interior angle is 120°, and its side equals the circumradius.
  • Converging lines: meeting angle = 180° minus the sum of the two same-side angles made by a transversal.

mcqs.q: To find the angle between converging lines without extending them, what do we do?
options: Add the two same-side angles to 180 degrees
Draw a transversal and subtract the sum of the two same-side angles from 180 degrees
Measure only one same-side angle and double it
Extend both lines backwards and measure with a ruler
mcqs.why: The correct method is to draw a transversal and subtract the sum of the two same-side angles from 180 degrees, because those angles and the meeting angle together make a straight line total.

mcqs.q: To construct a square from its diagonal AC = 6 cm, which step comes after drawing AC?
options: Draw a circle with centre A
Make a 108 degree angle at A
Draw the perpendicular bisector of AC
Draw perpendiculars at A and C
mcqs.why: The correct next step is to draw the perpendicular bisector of AC, because the other two vertices B and D of the square lie on it, equally distant from the midpoint.

mcqs.q: In the square-from-diagonal construction with AC = 6 cm, the arcs that give B and D are drawn with centre P (the midpoint) and radius equal to:
mcqs.why: The correct radius is PA = 3 cm, half of the 6 cm diagonal, because the diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other at P.

mcqs.q: To construct a square with side BC = 7 cm, the arcs cutting the perpendiculars at B and C are drawn with radius:
mcqs.why: The correct radius is 7 cm, the same as the side, because every side of a square is equal, so the arcs from B and C must cut off 7 cm on the perpendiculars.

mcqs.q: What is the side of a square whose diagonal is 8 cm?
mcqs.why: The correct side is 8 divided by root 2, about 5.66 cm, because in a square the diagonal is the side multiplied by root 2.

mcqs.q: To construct rectangle PQRS with PQ = 6 cm and QR = 4 cm, after drawing PQ and the perpendiculars at P and Q, the arcs are drawn with radius:
mcqs.why: The correct radius is 4 cm, the length QR, because the arcs from P and Q must cut the perpendiculars at S and R, exactly the width of the rectangle.

mcqs.q: A rectangle is given by side AB = 4 cm and diagonal AC = 6 cm. How is point C found?
options: With an arc of radius 6 cm centred at A, cutting the perpendicular at B
With an arc of radius 4 cm centred at B
With the perpendicular bisector of AB
By making a 60 degree angle at B
mcqs.why: Point C is found with an arc of radius 6 cm centred at A cutting the perpendicular at B, because AC is the given 6 cm diagonal from A to C.

mcqs.q: For that rectangle (AB = 4 cm, diagonal 6 cm), the other side BC is:
mcqs.why: The correct length is root of (36 - 16) = root 20, about 4.47 cm, found by Pythagoras in the right triangle formed by the side, the other side and the diagonal.

mcqs.q: To construct a rhombus with side 4 cm and angle A = 120 degrees, point C is found by arcs of radius 4 cm centred at:
mcqs.why: Point C is found by arcs of radius 4 cm centred at B and D, because in a rhombus all sides are 4 cm, so C is 4 cm from both B and D.

mcqs.q: In that rhombus with angle A = 120 degrees, angles B and D are each:
mcqs.why: Angles B and D are each 60 degrees, because consecutive angles of a rhombus are supplementary (180 - 120 = 60) and opposite angles are equal.

mcqs.q: To construct a rhombus from side PQ = 5 cm and diagonal QS = 4 cm, P and R are found on:
options: The perpendicular bisector of QS, using arcs of radius 5 cm from Q and S
A line parallel to QS at 5 cm
The extension of QS beyond S
mcqs.why: P and R lie on the perpendicular bisector of QS, found by arcs of radius 5 cm centred at Q and S, because each is one side (5 cm) away from both ends of the diagonal.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram is built from diagonals PR = 6 cm and QS = 8 cm crossing at 120 degrees. The halves used at the midpoint O are:
options: OP = OR = 6 cm and OQ = OS = 8 cm
All four halves equal to 5 cm
OP = OR = 4 cm and OQ = OS = 3 cm
OP = OR = 3 cm and OQ = OS = 4 cm
mcqs.why: The correct halves are OP = OR = 3 cm and OQ = OS = 4 cm, because the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so each diagonal is halved at O.

mcqs.q: To construct parallelogram ABCD with AB = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm and angle B = 70 degrees, the last vertex D is found by arcs centred at A and C with radii:
options: BC (4 cm) from A and AB (6 cm) from C
10 cm from both A and C
mcqs.why: D is found with radius BC = 4 cm from A and radius AB = 6 cm from C, because the side opposite AB equals AB and the side opposite BC equals BC in a parallelogram.

mcqs.q: Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is:
mcqs.why: Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is 108 degrees, from (2 x 5 - 4) x 90 degrees divided by 5, and the construction makes 108 degree angles at A and B.

mcqs.q: To construct a regular hexagon of side 3 cm, we draw a circle of radius 3 cm and mark off arcs around it. This works because in a regular hexagon:
mcqs.why: The method works because the circumradius equals the side in a regular hexagon, so stepping the same 3 cm radius around the circle gives all six vertices, and each interior angle is 120 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.2
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

This exercise constructs right-angled triangles. The key fact is that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle: if the hypotenuse is taken as the diameter of a semicircle (or circle), then any point A on the semicircle gives angle A = 90°. This one idea solves most of the constructions in this exercise.

When the two sides around the right angle are given instead, we simply draw a perpendicular at the vertex and cut the second side on it.

Steps of Construction — Right Triangle from the Hypotenuse and One Side (for example, hypotenuse = 10 cm, one side = 8 cm)

  1. Draw hypotenuse BC = 10 cm.
  2. Taking BC as diameter, draw a semicircle on it.
  3. With centre B and radius 8 cm, draw an arc cutting the semicircle at A.
  4. Join AB and AC.

For hypotenuse 13 cm and one side 12 cm, use the same steps: a semicircle on BC = 13 cm, and A from an arc of radius 12 cm centred at B.

Steps of Construction — Right Triangle from Two Sides (for example, PQ = 5 cm, SQ = 6 cm)

  1. Draw PQ = 5 cm.
  2. Draw a perpendicular at Q and cut QS = 6 cm on it.
  3. Join P and S.

Steps of Construction — Right Triangle from the Hypotenuse and the Altitude to the Hypotenuse (for example, hypotenuse = 10 cm, altitude = 3 cm)

  1. Draw hypotenuse BC = 10 cm.
  2. Taking BC as diameter, draw a semicircle on it.
  3. Draw a line parallel to BC at a distance of 3 cm from BC, cutting the semicircle at A.
  4. Join AB and AC.

For hypotenuse 12 cm and altitude 4 cm, use the same steps with a line parallel to BC at a distance of 4 cm. The parallel line gives the correct height, and the semicircle gives the right angle.

Steps of Construction — Two Right Triangles on a Common Hypotenuse (BC = 10 cm, altitude AL = 3.5 cm, DC = 5 cm)

  1. Draw the common hypotenuse BC = 10 cm.
  2. Taking BC as diameter, draw a circle on it.
  3. Draw a line parallel to BC at a distance of 3.5 cm from BC, cutting the circle at A on one side — triangle ABC is formed.
  4. With centre C and radius 5 cm, draw an arc cutting the circle at D on the other side — triangle DBC is formed.

For altitude AL = 3 cm and DB = 6 cm, use the same steps: A from a line parallel to BC at a distance of 3 cm, and D on the other side from an arc of radius 6 cm centred at B.

Remember

  • The angle in a semicircle is 90°, so the hypotenuse must be drawn first and used as the diameter.
  • Hypotenuse 10 cm and side 8 cm: the third side is √(100 - 64) = 6 cm.
  • Hypotenuse 13 cm and side 12 cm: the third side is √(169 - 144) = 5 cm.
  • Two sides 5 cm and 6 cm around the right angle: the hypotenuse is √(25 + 36) = √61, about 7.81 cm.
  • An altitude is given by a line parallel to the hypotenuse at exactly that distance from it.
  • For two triangles on a common hypotenuse, draw a full circle (not just a semicircle), because the two right-angle vertices lie on opposite sides of BC.
  • Check after construction: in triangle DBC with BC = 10 cm and DC = 5 cm, DB = √(100 - 25) = √75, about 8.66 cm; with DB = 6 cm, DC = √(100 - 36) = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: To construct a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm and one side 8 cm, the hypotenuse BC is first used as:
mcqs.why: BC is used as the diameter for a semicircle, because the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so any point A on it gives angle A = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: In that construction, point A is found by an arc of radius 8 cm centred at:
mcqs.why: Point A is found by an arc of radius 8 cm centred at B cutting the semicircle, because the given 8 cm side runs from B to A.

mcqs.q: For hypotenuse 10 cm and one side 8 cm, the third side is:
mcqs.why: The third side is 6 cm, from root of (100 - 64) = root 36, by Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle.

mcqs.q: For hypotenuse 13 cm and one side 12 cm, constructed the same way, the third side is:
mcqs.why: The third side is 5 cm, from root of (169 - 144) = root 25, which is the well-known 5-12-13 right triangle.

mcqs.q: A right triangle is given by the two sides PQ = 5 cm and SQ = 6 cm around the right angle at Q. The first steps are:
options: Draw a semicircle on PQ, then an arc from P
Draw the perpendicular bisector of PQ
Make a 60 degree angle at Q
Draw PQ = 5 cm, draw a perpendicular at Q, and cut QS = 6 cm on it
mcqs.why: The correct steps are to draw PQ = 5 cm, draw a perpendicular at Q and cut QS = 6 cm on it, because the right angle is at Q and the perpendicular gives exactly 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: For that triangle (sides 5 cm and 6 cm), the hypotenuse PS is:
mcqs.why: The hypotenuse is root of (25 + 36) = root 61, about 7.81 cm, by Pythagoras using the two sides around the right angle.

mcqs.q: To construct a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm and altitude from the hypotenuse equal to 3 cm, point A is found where:
options: A line parallel to BC at a distance of 3 cm cuts the semicircle on BC
An arc of radius 3 cm from B cuts BC
The perpendicular bisector of BC cuts the semicircle
A line parallel to BC at a distance of 10 cm cuts the semicircle
mcqs.why: Point A is where a line parallel to BC at a distance of 3 cm cuts the semicircle, because every point on that parallel line is exactly 3 cm above BC, giving the required altitude.

mcqs.q: Why does the semicircle method guarantee a right angle at A?
options: Because all radii of a circle are equal
Because the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees
Because parallel lines make right angles
Because the altitude bisects the hypotenuse
mcqs.why: The method works because the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees, so joining A to B and C always gives a right angle at A on the hypotenuse BC.

mcqs.q: Two right triangles ABC and DBC share the common hypotenuse BC = 10 cm. Why is a full circle drawn on BC instead of only a semicircle?
options: A circle is easier to draw than a semicircle
The altitude is measured from the centre
So that A and D can lie on opposite sides of BC
So that BC becomes a radius
mcqs.why: A full circle is drawn so that A and D can lie on opposite sides of BC, giving two different right triangles on the same hypotenuse, each right-angled by the angle in a semicircle.

mcqs.q: In triangle DBC on the common hypotenuse BC = 10 cm, with DC = 5 cm, the side DB is:
mcqs.why: DB is root of (100 - 25) = root 75, about 8.66 cm, by Pythagoras, since BC is the hypotenuse and DC is one side of the right triangle.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1 – Pythagoras' Theorem
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse. It is the longest side. The other two sides are the base and the perpendicular.

Pythagoras' theorem says that the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. To verify the theorem for given sides, square the hypotenuse on one side, add the squares of the other two sides on the other side, and check that both totals are equal.

(Hypotenuse)2 = (Base)2 + (Perpendicular)2

Worked Example

Verify Pythagoras' theorem for triangle PQR with PQ = 12 cm, QR = 5 cm, PR = 13 cm.

Step 1: The longest side is PR = 13 cm, so PR is the hypotenuse.

Step 2: Square the hypotenuse: 132 = 169.

Step 3: Square the first leg: 122 = 144.

Step 4: Square the second leg: 52 = 25.

Step 5: Add the two leg squares: 144 + 25 = 169.

Step 6: Compare: 169 = 169.

Step 7: Both sides are equal, so Pythagoras' theorem is verified.

Remember

  • The hypotenuse is always the longest side, opposite the 90 degree angle.
  • Always square the hypotenuse alone on one side and add the squares of the other two sides on the other side.
  • Useful triples in this exercise: 3 cm, 3 cm, 3√2 cm; 5 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm; 1.2 cm, 1.6 cm, 2 cm; 9 cm, 12 cm, 15 cm; 12 cm, 16 cm, 20 cm; 15 cm, 20 cm, 25 cm.
  • If the two totals are equal, the theorem is verified; if they are not equal, it is not verified.

mcqs.q: For the triangle with sides 3 cm, 3 cm and 3√2 cm, what is (3√2)²?
mcqs.why: (3√2)² = 9 x 2 = 18. This is the hypotenuse square in Exercise 9.1, and it equals 3² + 3² = 18, so the theorem is verified.

mcqs.q: In triangle PQR with PQ = 12 cm, QR = 5 cm, PR = 13 cm, which side is the hypotenuse?
mcqs.why: The hypotenuse is the longest side, PR = 13 cm. Checking: 13² = 169 and 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169, so PR is correctly the hypotenuse.

mcqs.q: What is 12² + 5²?
mcqs.why: 12² = 144 and 5² = 25, so 144 + 25 = 169. This equals 13², which is why the 5 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm triangle verifies Pythagoras' theorem.

mcqs.q: For sides 1.2 cm, 1.6 cm and 2 cm, what is 1.6² + 1.2²?
mcqs.why: 1.6² = 2.56 and 1.2² = 1.44, so 2.56 + 1.44 = 4.00. This equals 2² = 4, so the triangle with hypotenuse 2 cm verifies the theorem.

mcqs.q: In triangle LMN with angle M = 90 degrees, LM = 9 cm, MN = 12 cm, LN = 15 cm, what is 9² + 12²?
mcqs.why: 9² = 81 and 12² = 144, so 81 + 144 = 225. This equals 15² = 225, with hypotenuse LN = 15 cm, so the theorem is verified.

mcqs.q: In triangle PQR with angle Q = 90 degrees, PQ = 16 cm, QR = 12 cm, PR = 20 cm, what is (20)²?
mcqs.why: The hypotenuse is PR = 20 cm and 20² = 400. Also 16² + 12² = 256 + 144 = 400, so both sides match and the theorem is verified.

mcqs.q: In triangle XYZ with angle Y = 90 degrees, XY = 15 cm, YZ = 20 cm, XZ = 25 cm, what is 15² + 20²?
mcqs.why: 15² = 225 and 20² = 400, so 225 + 400 = 625. This equals 25² = 625, with hypotenuse XZ = 25 cm, verifying Pythagoras' theorem.

mcqs.q: Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right triangle:
mcqs.why: The correct statement uses squares added together for the hypotenuse. Every verification in Exercise 9.1 uses exactly this form, with squares, not a plain sum.

mcqs.q: For the 3 cm, 3 cm, 3√2 cm triangle, what is the sum of the squares of the two 3 cm sides?
mcqs.why: Each 3 cm side squared is 9, so the sum is 9 + 9 = 18. This matches the hypotenuse square of 18, which is how Exercise 9.1 verifies this triangle.

mcqs.q: Which equality correctly verifies the triangle with sides 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm?
mcqs.why: 81 + 144 = 225, so the squares of 9 and 12 add to the square of 15. The longest side 15 cm must be the hypotenuse in Pythagoras' theorem.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.2 – Finding Unknown Sides
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

This exercise uses Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side. If both legs are known, add their squares to get the hypotenuse. If the hypotenuse and one leg are known, subtract the squares to get the other leg. Then take the square root.

The same test decides whether three given lengths form a right triangle: square the largest length and compare it with the sum of the squares of the other two. Equal means a right triangle; not equal means it is not a right triangle.

For an isosceles right triangle the two equal sides give H squared = 2 x (side) squared, so (side) squared = H squared divided by 2.

(Hypotenuse)2 = (Base)2 + (Perpendicular)2

Unknown leg: (leg)2 = (hypotenuse)2 − (known leg)2

Isosceles right triangle: (side)2 = H2 ÷ 2

Diagonal of a rectangle: (diagonal)2 = (length)2 + (width)2

Worked Example

A ladder 6.5 m long reaches a height of 5.2 m on a wall. Find the distance of the foot of the ladder from the wall.

Step 1: The ladder is the hypotenuse, 6.5 m. The height on the wall is one leg, 5.2 m.

Step 2: Write (distance) squared = (hypotenuse) squared minus (height) squared.

Step 3: (distance) squared = 6.5 squared minus 5.2 squared.

Step 4: 6.5 squared = 42.25 and 5.2 squared = 27.04.

Step 5: Subtract: 42.25 minus 27.04 = 15.21.

Step 6: Take the square root: distance = square root of 15.21 = 3.9 m.

So the foot of the ladder is 3.9 m from the wall.

Remember

  • Add squares to find the hypotenuse; subtract squares to find a leg; always take the square root at the end.
  • To test for a right triangle, always use the largest side as the possible hypotenuse.
  • Sets that form right triangles in this exercise include 9, 12, 15; 6, 8, 10; 12, 16, 20; 1.5, 2, 2.5. Sets 7, 8, 9 and 2, 4, 6 do not.
  • Rectangle diagonal, ladder, pole-and-wire and shortcut-path problems are all Pythagoras problems in disguise.
  • For a plot with width 48 m and diagonal 80 m, the length is 64 m and the area is 64 x 48 = 3072 square metres.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 12 cm. What is the hypotenuse?
mcqs.why: x squared = 81 + 144 = 225, so x = 15 cm. Add the leg squares to find the hypotenuse, then take the square root, as in Exercise 9.2.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 25 cm and one leg 15 cm. What is the other leg?
mcqs.why: y squared = 625 minus 225 = 400, so y = 20 cm. Subtract the squares when a leg is missing, do not add them, in this Exercise 9.2 problem.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has legs 4.5 cm and 6 cm. What is the hypotenuse?
mcqs.why: z squared = 20.25 + 36 = 56.25, so z = 7.5 cm. This is the hypotenuse for legs 4.5 cm and 6 cm in Exercise 9.2, Question 1.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has legs 4.8 cm and 3.6 cm. What is the hypotenuse?
mcqs.why: x squared = 23.04 + 12.96 = 36, so x = 6 cm. The two decimal legs still give a whole-number hypotenuse in this Exercise 9.2 case.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 8 cm and one leg 6.4 cm. What is the other leg?
mcqs.why: s squared = 64 minus 40.96 = 23.04, so s = 4.8 cm. Subtract to find the missing leg in this triangle from Exercise 9.2.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has legs 2.1 cm and 2.8 cm. What is the hypotenuse?
mcqs.why: r squared = 4.41 + 7.84 = 12.25, so r = 3.5 cm. This is the hypotenuse for legs 2.1 cm and 2.8 cm in Exercise 9.2.

mcqs.q: Do the lengths 7, 8 and 9 form a right triangle?
options: Yes, the squares match with hypotenuse 9
Yes, the squares match with hypotenuse 8
mcqs.why: 49 + 64 = 113, not 81, and the other two comparisons also fail in the book. So 7, 8 and 9 do not form a right triangle.

mcqs.q: Do the lengths 6, 8 and 10 form a right triangle?
mcqs.why: 36 + 64 = 100, which equals 10 squared, so the equality holds with hypotenuse 10. Therefore 6, 8 and 10 do form a right triangle.

mcqs.q: Do the lengths 2, 4 and 6 form a right triangle?
options: Only if the right angle is at side 4
mcqs.why: 4 + 16 = 20, not 36, and the other comparisons also fail in the book. So 2, 4 and 6 do not form a right triangle in Exercise 9.2.

mcqs.q: The square of the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 50 square cm. What is one equal side?
mcqs.why: For an isosceles right triangle, side squared = 50 divided by 2 = 25, so the side is 5 cm. Halve first, then take the square root.

mcqs.q: The square of the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 72 square cm. What is one equal side?
mcqs.why: Side squared = 72 divided by 2 = 36, so the side is 6 cm. This matches Exercise 9.2 for hypotenuse squared equal to 72.

mcqs.q: A ladder 6.5 m long reaches 5.2 m up a wall. How far is its foot from the wall?
mcqs.why: Distance squared = 42.25 minus 27.04 = 15.21, so distance = 3.9 m. The ladder itself is the hypotenuse in this Exercise 9.2 problem.

mcqs.q: A pole is 12 m high. A 20 m wire from its top is tied to a peg on the ground. How far is the peg from the pole?
mcqs.why: Distance squared = 400 minus 144 = 256, so distance = 16 m. The wire is the hypotenuse in this pole problem from Exercise 9.2.

mcqs.q: What is the diagonal of a rectangle with length 6 m and width 8 m?
mcqs.why: Diagonal squared = 36 + 64 = 100, so diagonal = 10 m. A rectangle diagonal is found with Pythagoras theorem in Exercise 9.2.

mcqs.q: A rectangular plot has width 48 m and diagonal 80 m. What is its area?
mcqs.why: Length squared = 6400 minus 2304 = 4096, so length = 64 m. Area = 64 x 48 = 3072 square metres, as in Exercise 9.2.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.3 – Heron's Formula
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

Heron's formula finds the area of any triangle when all three sides are known, even when the height is not given. First find S, the semi-perimeter, which is half the perimeter. Then use S together with (S minus a), (S minus b) and (S minus c) inside a square root.

S = (a + b + c) ÷ 2

Area = square root of [S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)]

Area of an equilateral triangle = (square root of 3 ÷ 4) x a squared

If S and two sides are known, the third side is c = 2S minus a minus b, because 2S = a + b + c.

Worked Example

Find the area of a triangle with sides d = 10 cm, e = 17 cm, f = 21 cm.

Step 1: Add the sides: 10 + 17 + 21 = 48.

Step 2: Find S: S = 48 ÷ 2 = 24.

Step 3: Find S minus d = 24 minus 10 = 14.

Step 4: Find S minus e = 24 minus 17 = 7.

Step 5: Find S minus f = 24 minus 21 = 3.

Step 6: Multiply inside the root: 24 x 14 x 7 x 3 = 7056.

Step 7: Take the square root: Area = square root of 7056 = 84 square cm.

Remember

  • Always find S first: S is half the sum of the three sides, never the full sum.
  • The four factors inside the root are S, (S minus a), (S minus b) and (S minus c), all multiplied together.
  • For an isosceles triangle two factors are equal, for example sides 10 cm, 10 cm, 12 cm give area 48 square cm.
  • A right triangle can also be checked by Heron: sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm give S = 12 and area 24 square cm.
  • Area is always in square units, such as square cm.

mcqs.q: For a triangle with sides 16 cm, 20 cm and 16 cm, what is S?
mcqs.why: S = (16 + 20 + 16) divided by 2 = 52 divided by 2 = 26. S is the semi-perimeter, half the perimeter, as used in Heron's formula.

mcqs.q: What is the area of a triangle with sides 10 cm, 17 cm and 21 cm? (S = 24)
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (24 x 14 x 7 x 3) = square root of 7056 = 84 square cm. The value 7056 is still inside the root and must be square-rooted.

mcqs.q: What is the area of a triangle with sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm? (S = 12)
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (12 x 6 x 4 x 2) = square root of 576 = 24 square cm. This agrees with half x 6 x 8 for this right triangle.

mcqs.q: What is the area of an isosceles triangle with sides 10 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm? (S = 16)
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (16 x 6 x 6 x 4) = square root of 2304 = 48 square cm. The two equal sides give two equal factors of 6 here.

mcqs.q: By Heron's formula, the area of an equilateral triangle with side a is:
mcqs.why: With S = 3a over 2, the area simplifies to (root 3 over 4) times a squared. This is the equilateral result proved in Exercise 9.3, Question 3.

mcqs.q: In Heron's formula, S is equal to:
mcqs.why: S = (a + b + c) divided by 2, the semi-perimeter. Forgetting to divide by 2 is the most common slip in Heron's formula questions.

mcqs.q: Heron's formula for the area of a triangle is:
options: Root of S(S plus a)(S plus b)(S plus c)
S(S minus a)(S minus b)(S minus c) without a root
Half times S times (a plus b plus c)
Root of S(S minus a)(S minus b)(S minus c)
mcqs.why: Area = square root of S(S minus a)(S minus b)(S minus c), with minus signs and a square root. This is exactly the formula used in Exercise 9.3.

mcqs.q: Given a = 13 cm, b = 15 cm and S = 20 cm, what is the third side c?
mcqs.why: c = 2S minus a minus b = 40 minus 13 minus 15 = 12 cm. Since 2S = a + b + c, the missing side follows directly in Exercise 9.3.

mcqs.q: For a = 13 cm, b = 15 cm, c = 12 cm and S = 20 cm, what is the area?
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (20 x 7 x 5 x 8) = square root of 5600 = 20 root 14, about 74.83 square cm. The number 5600 must still be square-rooted.

mcqs.q: For a triangle with sides 15 cm, 21 cm and 14 cm, what is S?
mcqs.why: S = (15 + 21 + 14) divided by 2 = 50 divided by 2 = 25. Its area is then 10 root 110, about 104.88 square cm, in Exercise 9.3.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.4 – Area of a Quadrilateral
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

A quadrilateral has no single area formula from its four sides alone. The method in this exercise is to draw one diagonal. The diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles. Find the area of each triangle, usually with Heron's formula, and then add the two areas.

If a triangle formed this way is a right triangle, its area can be found faster with half base times height instead of Heron's formula.

Area of quadrilateral = Area of triangle 1 + Area of triangle 2

Heron: Area = square root of [S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)], S = (a + b + c) ÷ 2

Right triangle: Area = (1 ÷ 2) x base x height

Worked Example

Quadrilateral LMNO has LM = 5 cm, MN = 12 cm, LN = 13 cm, LO = 14 cm, NO = 15 cm. Find its area.

Step 1: Draw diagonal LN = 13 cm. It splits LMNO into triangles LMN and LNO.

Step 2: In triangle LMN, sides are 5 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm. Check: 25 + 144 = 169, so it is a right triangle.

Step 3: Area of triangle LMN = half x 5 x 12 = 30 square cm.

Step 4: In triangle LNO, sides are 14 cm, 15 cm, 13 cm. Find S = (14 + 15 + 13) divided by 2 = 21.

Step 5: Area of triangle LNO = square root of (21 x 7 x 6 x 8) = square root of 7056 = 84 square cm.

Step 6: Add the areas: Total area = 30 + 84 = 114 square cm.

Remember

  • Always split the quadrilateral with a diagonal whose length is given; never guess a diagonal length.
  • Check each triangle for a Pythagoras triple first, such as 3, 4, 5 or 5, 12, 13, because the half-base-times-height method is faster.
  • Quadrilateral ABCD (diagonal AC = 12 cm) has total area about 61.68 square cm; quadrilateral PQRS has total area 12 square cm.
  • Quadrilateral DEFG has total area about 199.36 square cm; the large plot UVWX has total area about 6549.65 square metres.
  • Keep units consistent: lengths in metres give area in square metres; lengths in centimetres give area in square cm.

mcqs.q: Quadrilateral ABCD is split by diagonal AC = 12 cm. Its two triangle areas are about 29.93 and 31.75 square cm. What is the total area?
mcqs.why: Total area = 29.93 + 31.75 = 61.68 square cm, approximately. A quadrilateral area is the sum of its two triangle areas after drawing a diagonal.

mcqs.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, triangle ABC has sides 10 cm, 6 cm, 12 cm with S = 14. What is its area?
options: 896 square cm as the final area
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (14 x 4 x 8 x 2) = square root of 896 = 8 root 14, about 29.93 square cm. The simplified surd form is the answer here.

mcqs.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, triangle ADC has sides 8 cm, 8 cm, 12 cm with S = 14. What is its area?
options: 1008 square cm as the final area
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (14 x 6 x 6 x 2) = square root of 1008 = 12 root 7, about 31.75 square cm. With triangle ABC it gives about 61.68 in total.

mcqs.q: Quadrilateral PQRS has diagonal PR = 5 cm, forming two 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm triangles. What is the total area?
mcqs.why: Each triangle is right-angled since 9 + 16 = 25, so each area = half x 3 x 4 = 6 square cm. Total = 6 + 6 = 12 square cm for quadrilateral PQRS.

mcqs.q: What is the area of one 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm right triangle in quadrilateral PQRS?
mcqs.why: Area = half x base x height = half x 3 x 4 = 6 square cm. Because 3, 4, 5 is a right triangle, Heron's formula is not needed for this part.

mcqs.q: Quadrilateral DEFG is split by diagonal DF = 25 cm. Its triangle areas are about 95.93 and 103.43 square cm. What is the total area?
mcqs.why: Total = 95.93 + 103.43 = 199.36 square cm, approximately. Both triangles share S = 28.5 in the book, and their areas must be added together.

mcqs.q: A quadrilateral plot UVWX has diagonal UW = 130 m. Triangle UVW has sides 120 m, 50 m, 130 m. What is its area?
mcqs.why: 2500 + 14400 = 16900, so it is a right triangle and area = half x 50 x 120 = 3000 square metres. Do not omit the half in this calculation.

mcqs.q: The plot UVWX has triangle areas 3000 and about 3549.65 square metres. What is the total area?
mcqs.why: Total = 3000 + 3549.65 = 6549.65 square metres, approximately. The second triangle uses Heron with S = 150 to give 600 root 35 square metres.

mcqs.q: Quadrilateral LMNO has triangle areas 30 and 84 square cm. What is its total area?
mcqs.why: Total = 30 + 84 = 114 square cm. Triangle LMN is the 5, 12, 13 right triangle giving 30, and triangle LNO gives 84 by Heron's formula.

mcqs.q: In quadrilateral LMNO, triangle LNO has sides 14 cm, 15 cm, 13 cm with S = 21. What is its area?
mcqs.why: Area = square root of (21 x 7 x 6 x 8) = square root of 7056 = 84 square cm. The value 7056 is under the root and must be square-rooted.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.5 – Surface Area and Volume of a Sphere
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

A sphere is a perfectly round solid, like a ball. It has one measurement, the radius r, from the centre to the surface. This exercise finds its surface area and its volume, and converts volume into litres of water. Use pi = 22/7 throughout this exercise.

To find r from a given surface area, use r squared = A divided by (4 pi) and then take the square root. Remember 1 litre = 1000 cubic cm and 1 cubic metre = 1000 litres.

Surface area of a sphere: A = 4 pi r squared

Volume of a sphere: V = (4 ÷ 3) pi r cubed

Radius from area: r squared = A x 7 ÷ 88 (when pi = 22/7)

Worked Example

Find the volume of a sphere with radius r = 21 cm.

Step 1: Write the formula: V = (4/3) pi r cubed.

Step 2: Put pi = 22/7 and r = 21: V = (4/3) x (22/7) x 21 cubed.

Step 3: Find 21 cubed = 21 x 21 x 21 = 9261.

Step 4: Combine the fractions: (4/3) x (22/7) = 88/21.

Step 5: Multiply: V = (88/21) x 9261.

Step 6: 9261 divided by 21 = 441, and 88 x 441 = 38808.

Step 7: So V = 38808 cubic cm.

Remember

  • Surface area uses r squared; volume uses r cubed. Mixing them is the most common error.
  • Doubling the radius makes the surface area 4 times and the volume 8 times.
  • If one radius is 3 times another, the areas are in ratio 9 : 1 and the volumes in ratio 27 : 1.
  • Convert carefully: divide cubic cm by 1000 to get litres; 1 cubic metre holds 1000 litres.
  • Melting problems keep the volume the same: a melted sphere's volume equals the total volume of what is made from it.

mcqs.q: What is the surface area of a sphere with radius 35 cm? (pi = 22/7)
mcqs.why: A = 4 pi r squared = 4 x (22/7) x 1225 = 15400 square cm. Surface area uses r squared with the factor 4 pi, as in Exercise 9.5.

mcqs.q: What is the surface area of a sphere with radius 56 cm? (pi = 22/7)
mcqs.why: A = 4 x (22/7) x 3136 = 39424 square cm. This is the surface area for radius 56 cm in Exercise 9.5, Question 1.

mcqs.q: A sphere has surface area 616 square cm. What is its radius?
mcqs.why: r squared = 616 x 7 divided by 88 = 49, so r = 7 cm. Work backwards from surface area = 4 pi r squared to find the radius.

mcqs.q: A sphere has surface area 2464 square cm. What is its radius?
mcqs.why: r squared = 2464 x 7 divided by 88 = 196, so r = 14 cm. This radius is also used again in the volume questions of Exercise 9.5.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a sphere with radius 21 cm?
mcqs.why: V = (4/3) x (22/7) x 9261 = 38808 cubic cm. Volume uses r cubed and the factor (4/3) pi, and its unit is cubic centimetres.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a sphere with radius 3.5 m?
mcqs.why: V = (88/21) x 42.875, about 179.67 cubic metres. This is the volume for radius 3.5 m in Exercise 9.5, Question 3.

mcqs.q: How many litres of water fit in a sphere of radius 70 cm? (Volume = 1437333.33 cubic cm)
mcqs.why: 1 litre = 1000 cubic cm, so 1437333.33 divided by 1000 is about 1437.33 litres. Always divide the cubic cm volume by 1000 to get litres.

mcqs.q: How many litres of water fit in a sphere of radius 105 cm? (Volume = 4851000 cubic cm)
mcqs.why: 4851000 divided by 1000 = 4851 litres exactly. This is the capacity for radius 105 cm in Exercise 9.5, Question 4.

mcqs.q: A sphere has surface area 2464 square cm, so r = 14 cm. What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (4/3) x (22/7) x 2744, about 11498.67 cubic cm, about 11.50 litres. First find r from the area, then use the volume formula.

mcqs.q: If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its surface area becomes:
mcqs.why: Area uses r squared, and (2r) squared = 4 r squared, so the new area is 4 times the old area. Area grows with the square of the radius.

mcqs.q: If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its volume becomes:
mcqs.why: Volume uses r cubed, and (2r) cubed = 8 r cubed, so the new volume is 8 times the old volume. Volume grows with the cube of the radius.

mcqs.q: Sphere A's radius is three times sphere B's radius. What is the ratio of their surface areas (A : B)?
mcqs.why: Area ratio = (3r) squared : r squared = 9 : 1. Square the radius ratio 3 to get the surface area ratio in Exercise 9.5, Question 7.

mcqs.q: Sphere A's radius is three times sphere B's radius. What is the ratio of their volumes (A : B)?
mcqs.why: Volume ratio = (3r) cubed : r cubed = 27 : 1. Cube the radius ratio 3 to get the volume ratio in Exercise 9.5, Question 7.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a football with radius 12 cm?
mcqs.why: V = (88/21) x 1728, about 7241.14 cubic cm. A football is treated as a sphere in Exercise 9.5, Question 10.

mcqs.q: A copper sphere of radius 7 cm (volume 1437.33 cubic cm) is melted into a wire of diameter 0.7 cm. What is the wire's length?
mcqs.why: Wire radius is 0.35 cm, wire volume = 0.385 x L, so L = 3733.33 cm = 37.33 m. Melting keeps the volume unchanged in this problem.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.6 – Surface Area and Volume of a Cone
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

A cone has a circular base of radius r, a vertical height h, and a slant height s along the sloping side. The three lengths form a right triangle, so s squared = r squared + h squared. The slant height is always longer than both r and h.

The base circle has its own area. The sloping side gives the curved surface area. Adding them gives the total surface area. The volume is one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.

Note on the source: in Exercise 9.6, Question 1, rows (iii) and (iv) give only one value each, so the cone cannot be found from them, and row (v) gives numbers that would make s smaller than r, which is impossible. Those three printed rows are not used in these notes or questions. In Question 4 the book prints the volume unit as square cm; it should be cubic cm.

Slant height: s squared = r squared + h squared

Circular (base) area: A1 = pi r squared

Curved surface area: A2 = pi r s

Total surface area: A = pi r (r + s) = A1 + A2

Volume of a cone: V = (1 ÷ 3) pi r squared h

Worked Example

A cone has r = 21 cm and h = 28 cm. Find s and the total surface area.

Step 1: Find s: s = square root of (28 squared + 21 squared).

Step 2: 28 squared = 784 and 21 squared = 441.

Step 3: Add: 784 + 441 = 1225.

Step 4: Take the square root: s = square root of 1225 = 35 cm.

Step 5: Base area A1 = pi r squared = (22/7) x 441 = 1386 square cm.

Step 6: Curved area A2 = pi r s = (22/7) x 21 x 35 = 2310 square cm.

Step 7: Total area A = 1386 + 2310 = 3696 square cm.

Remember

  • Always find s first with s squared = r squared + h squared; s must be greater than r and greater than h.
  • Base area uses r squared; curved area uses r times s; total area is their sum.
  • Volume has the factor 1/3: forgetting it makes the answer three times too big.
  • If the base area is given, volume can be found as (1/3) x (base area) x h.
  • Volume is in cubic units; surface area is in square units.

mcqs.q: A cone has r = 21 cm and h = 28 cm. What is the slant height s?
mcqs.why: s = square root of (784 + 441) = square root of 1225 = 35 cm. Slant height comes from Pythagoras on r and h for the cone.

mcqs.q: For a cone with r = 21 cm, what is the circular base area A1?
mcqs.why: A1 = pi r squared = (22/7) x 441 = 1386 square cm. The base area uses r squared only, not the slant height, in Exercise 9.6.

mcqs.q: For a cone with r = 21 cm and s = 35 cm, what is the curved surface area A2?
mcqs.why: A2 = pi r s = (22/7) x 21 x 35 = 2310 square cm. Curved area uses r times s, which is different from the base area pi r squared.

mcqs.q: For a cone with r = 21 cm and s = 35 cm, what is the total surface area?
mcqs.why: Total A = A1 + A2 = 1386 + 2310 = 3696 square cm. Both the base and curved parts must be added for the total surface area.

mcqs.q: A cone has h = 56 cm and s = 70 cm. What is the radius r?
mcqs.why: r = square root of (4900 minus 3136) = square root of 1764 = 42 cm. Subtract the squares to recover r from s and h here.

mcqs.q: For a cone with r = 42 cm and s = 70 cm, what is the total surface area?
mcqs.why: A1 = 5544 and A2 = 9240, so total = 5544 + 9240 = 14784 square cm. This is the total for h = 56 cm, s = 70 cm in Exercise 9.6.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a cone with r = 3 cm and h = 7 cm?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 9 x 7 = 66 cubic cm. Without the 1/3 factor you would wrongly get 198, three times too large.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a cone with r = 3.5 cm and h = 6 cm?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 12.25 x 6 = 77 cubic cm. This is the volume for r = 3.5 cm, h = 6 cm in Exercise 9.6, Question 2.

mcqs.q: A cone has h = 28 cm and s = 35 cm, so r = 21 cm. What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 441 x 28 = 12936 cubic cm. First recover r = 21 cm from s and h, then use the cone volume formula.

mcqs.q: A cone has base area 2464 square cm (so r = 28 cm) and height three times the radius (h = 84 cm). What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (base area) x h = (1/3) x 2464 x 84 = 68992 cubic cm. Using the given base area directly avoids finding r squared again.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.7 – Applied Volumes
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

This exercise applies the sphere and cone volume formulas to real objects: a ball, an ice-cream cup, a tent, and tanks holding wheat or water. The method is always the same: choose the correct volume formula, put in r and h, calculate carefully, and then convert if the question asks for kilograms or litres.

For the wheat tank, 1 cubic metre holds 100 kg of wheat. For water, 1 cubic metre = 1000 litres.

Volume of a sphere: V = (4 ÷ 3) pi r cubed

Volume of a cone: V = (1 ÷ 3) pi r squared h

Worked Example

A conical tank has height 7 m and radius 6 m. How much wheat will it hold, if 1 cubic metre holds 100 kg of wheat?

Step 1: Write the cone formula: V = (1/3) pi r squared h.

Step 2: Put pi = 22/7, r = 6, h = 7: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 36 x 7.

Step 3: Find 6 squared = 36 (already used above).

Step 4: The 7 in h cancels the 7 in 22/7: V = (1/3) x 22 x 36.

Step 5: 22 x 36 = 792, and 792 divided by 3 = 264.

Step 6: So V = 264 cubic metres.

Step 7: Wheat = 264 x 100 = 26400 kg.

Remember

  • A sphere of radius 7 cm has volume 1437.33 cubic cm; the same value appears for the melted copper sphere in Exercise 9.5.
  • A conical cup with r = 6 cm, h = 10.5 cm holds 396 cubic cm of ice cream.
  • Read the question to the end: volume alone, litres of water, and kilograms of wheat are three different final answers.
  • For a football with volume 9 pi over 16 cubic cm, solving for r gives r cubed = 27/64, so r = 3/4 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a sphere with radius 7 cm?
mcqs.why: V = (4/3) x (22/7) x 343, about 1437.33 cubic cm. This is the sphere volume asked in Exercise 9.7, Question 1, using pi = 22/7.

mcqs.q: A conical cup has radius 6 cm and height 10.5 cm. How much ice cream does it hold?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 36 x 10.5 = 396 cubic cm. The cup is a cone, so the 1/3 factor in the volume formula must be included.

mcqs.q: A conical tent has height 4.2 m and base radius 5.6 m. What is the volume of air inside?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 31.36 x 4.2 = 137.984, about 137.98 cubic metres. This is the air volume of the conical tent in Exercise 9.7.

mcqs.q: A conical tank has height 7 m and radius 6 m. What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 36 x 7 = 264 cubic metres. This volume is then used to find the wheat mass in the next part of the question.

mcqs.q: The tank above (volume 264 cubic metres) holds wheat at 100 kg per cubic metre. How much wheat does it hold?
mcqs.why: Wheat = 264 x 100 = 26400 kg. Multiply the volume in cubic metres by 100 kg per cubic metre, as stated in Exercise 9.7, Question 4.

mcqs.q: A conical water tank has height 7 m and base radius 3 m. What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 9 x 7 = 66 cubic metres. This is the volume of the conical water tank in Exercise 9.7, Question 5.

mcqs.q: How many litres of water can the tank above (volume 66 cubic metres) hold?
mcqs.why: 1 cubic metre = 1000 litres, so 66 x 1000 = 66000 litres. Convert cubic metres to litres by multiplying by 1000, not by 100.

mcqs.q: A conical tank is 6.3 m high with base radius 8.4 m. What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) x (22/7) x 70.56 x 6.3 = 465.696, about 465.70 cubic metres. This is the tank volume in Exercise 9.7, Question 6.

mcqs.q: A football has volume 9 pi over 16 cubic cm. What is its radius?
mcqs.why: From the sphere formula, r cubed = 27/64, so r = 3/4 cm. Take the cube root at the end, not the value of r cubed itself.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cone is given by:
mcqs.why: Cone volume is (1/3) pi r squared h. The formula without 1/3 is a cylinder volume, and (4/3) pi r cubed belongs to a sphere.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 9
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

The Review Exercise tests the whole unit in short multiple-choice form: Pythagoras for rectangle diagonals and missing perpendiculars, Heron's formula and the meaning of S, the sphere area and volume formulas, the value of pi, and basic cone facts. Each question needs only the correct formula or one short calculation.

Note on the source: Review Question 10 prints its answer choices with the unit cubic metres, but a total surface area must be in square metres. The value 44 is correct; only the printed unit is wrong. These notes use square metres for that area.

Diagonal: (diagonal) squared = (length) squared + (width) squared

Heron: Area = square root of [S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)], S = (a + b + c) ÷ 2

Sphere: A = 4 pi r squared, V = (4 ÷ 3) pi r cubed

Cone: V = (1 ÷ 3) pi r squared h, base area = pi r squared, total area = pi r (r + s)

Worked Example

A rectangle has length 8 cm and width 6 cm. Find its diagonal.

Step 1: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 cm and 6 cm.

Step 2: Write (diagonal) squared = 8 squared + 6 squared.

Step 3: 8 squared = 64 and 6 squared = 36.

Step 4: Add: 64 + 36 = 100.

Step 5: Take the square root: diagonal = square root of 100 = 10 cm.

So the correct choice is 10 cm.

Remember

  • A right triangle with base 9 cm and hypotenuse 15 cm has perpendicular 12 cm, since 225 minus 81 = 144.
  • Pi is approximately 22/7 = 3 and 1/7, the value used throughout this unit.
  • A cone with r = 1, h = 3 has volume pi; its circular base with r = 1 has area pi square metres.
  • Watch units in review questions: areas are in square units and volumes in cubic units.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has length 8 cm and width 6 cm. What is its diagonal?
mcqs.why: Diagonal = square root of (64 + 36) = square root of 100 = 10 cm. This is Review Exercise 9, Question 1, a direct Pythagoras calculation.

mcqs.q: Right triangle ABC has base 9 cm and hypotenuse 15 cm. What is the perpendicular?
mcqs.why: Perpendicular = square root of (225 minus 81) = square root of 144 = 12 cm. Subtract the squares to find the missing leg here.

mcqs.q: According to Heron's formula, the area of a triangle is:
options: Root of S(S plus a)(S plus b)(S plus c)
Root of S plus separate terms without multiplication
Root of S(S minus a)(S minus b)(S minus c)
Root of S(S minus a minus b minus c)
mcqs.why: Heron's formula is the square root of S(S minus a)(S minus b)(S minus c), option (ii) in the book. All three factors use minus signs inside one root.

mcqs.q: The value of S used in Heron's formula is:
options: S = (a minus b minus c) over 2
S = (a plus b minus c) over 2
S = (a plus b plus c) over 3
S = (a plus b plus c) over 2
mcqs.why: S = (a + b + c) over 2, the semi-perimeter, option (iii) in the book. Divide the full perimeter by 2, not by 3, and include all three sides.

mcqs.q: The formula for the surface area of a sphere is:
mcqs.why: Sphere surface area is A = 4 pi r squared, option (iv) in the book. The factor is 4, not 1, 2 or 3, and the power of r is 2 for area.

mcqs.q: The formula for the volume of a sphere is:
mcqs.why: Sphere volume is V = (4/3) pi r cubed, option (iv) in the book. Both the fraction 4/3 and the cube of r are needed for volume.

mcqs.q: The value of pi is approximately:
mcqs.why: Pi is approximately 22/7 = 3 and 1/7, option (i) in the book. This is the same value pi = 22/7 used in all calculations of this unit.

mcqs.q: A cone has r = 1 and h = 3. What is its volume?
mcqs.why: V = (1/3) pi x 1 x 3 = pi, and as a volume its unit is cubic metres, so the answer is pi cubic metres, option (i) in Review Exercise 9.

mcqs.q: A cone has radius 1 m. What is the area of its circular base?
mcqs.why: Base area = pi r squared = pi x 1 = pi, and as an area its unit is square metres, so the answer is pi square metres, option (ii) in the book.

mcqs.q: A cone has slant height 5 m and radius 2 m. What is its total surface area value? (Area unit is square metres)
mcqs.why: Total area = pi r (r + s) = pi x 2 x 7 = 14 pi, about 44, in square metres. The book prints cubic metres for the choices, but an area must be in square metres.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2
lessons.notes_html:
Opening — Basic Parts of a Proof (Exercise 10.1)

From Exercise 10.1: The basic parts of a proof are six: (1) Statement — what is to be proved, (2) Given — what is given, (3) Required to prove — stating clearly what is to be proved, (4) Construction — an addition to the figure if needed, (5) Proof — proving by logical reasoning, (6) Q.E.D. (proved).

Every proof in this unit follows this order. First read the statement, then note what is given, then say clearly what is required to prove, add any construction, and then give the proof step by step.

Concept

Theorem 1: The sum of the angles formed at any point on a straight line is 180 degrees (2 right angles). Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary, so their measures add to 180 degrees.

Two angles are supplementary if their measures add to 180 degrees. Two angles are complementary if their measures add to 90 degrees. In the figure for Question 1, lines form angle BOC with a straight line and a perpendicular ray OP. The supplementary angle of angle BOC is angle AOC, because angle BOC and angle AOC are a pair of adjacent angles on a straight line. The complementary angle of angle BOC is angle POC, because line OP is perpendicular to AB, so angle BOC and angle POC together make 90 degrees.

Worked example: If m angle BOC = 50 degrees, its complementary angle = 90 degrees - 50 degrees = 40 degrees, and its supplementary angle = 180 degrees - 50 degrees = 130 degrees.

Worked example: If m angle BOC = 45 degrees, m angle COD = 3x and m angle AOC = 2x, the three angles are on the same side of a straight line, so by Corollary 1 of Theorem 1, 2x + 3x + 45 degrees = 180 degrees, so 5x = 135 degrees and x = 27 degrees. Hence m angle COD = 81 degrees and m angle AOC = 54 degrees.

Worked example: When two lines cross, opposite angles are vertical angles and are equal. If m angle BOC = 40 degrees, then m angle AOC = 180 degrees - 40 degrees = 140 degrees, m angle BOD, the vertical angle of angle AOC, is 140 degrees, and m angle AOD, the vertical angle of angle BOC, is 40 degrees. If m angle BOC = 45 degrees, then m angle AOC = 135 degrees, m angle BOD = 135 degrees and m angle AOD = 45 degrees.

Proof — Bisectors of Adjacent Supplementary Angles Are Perpendicular

Statement: The bisectors of two adjacent supplementary angles are perpendicular to each other.

Given: Angle AOC and angle BOC are two adjacent supplementary angles. OE bisects angle AOC and OD bisects angle BOC.

To Prove: OE is perpendicular to OD, that is, m angle EOD = 90 degrees.

Construction: No extra construction; the figure shows the two adjacent angles on a straight line with their bisectors OE and OD.

Proof:

By Theorem 1, m angle AOC + m angle BOC = 180 degrees.

Dividing both sides by 2: (1/2) m angle AOC + (1/2) m angle BOC = 90 degrees.

That is, m angle EOC + m angle DOC = 90 degrees, because OE and OD are the bisectors.

But m angle EOC + m angle DOC = m angle EOD.

So m angle EOD = 90 degrees, that is, OE perpendicular to OD.

Q.E.D.

Proof — If Bisectors Are Perpendicular, the Angles Are Supplementary

Statement: If the bisectors of two adjacent angles are perpendicular to each other, then the two angles are supplementary.

Given: OE and OD are the bisectors of angle AOC and angle BOC, and OE is perpendicular to OD, that is, m angle EOD = 90 degrees.

To Prove: Angle AOC and angle BOC are supplementary, that is, m angle AOC + m angle BOC = 180 degrees.

Construction: No extra construction; the figure shows the two adjacent angles with bisectors OE and OD.

Proof:

m angle EOD = m angle EOC + m angle DOC.

m angle EOC + m angle DOC = (1/2) m angle AOC + (1/2) m angle BOC = 90 degrees.

Multiplying both sides by 2: m angle AOC + m angle BOC = 180 degrees.

That is, angle AOC and angle BOC are supplementary.

Q.E.D.

In the figure of Question 4, if m angle AOE = m angle EOC = a and m angle BOD = m angle DOC = b, then a + b = 90 degrees. Hence the complementary pairs are: (angle AOE, angle BOD), (angle BOD, angle COE), (angle DOC, angle COE), (angle DOC, angle AOE) — each pair sums to a + b = 90 degrees.

Remember

  • The six parts of a proof are Statement, Given, Required to prove, Construction, Proof and Q.E.D.
  • Supplementary angles add to 180 degrees; complementary angles add to 90 degrees.
  • Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary by Theorem 1.
  • If m angle BOC = 50 degrees, complement is 40 degrees and supplement is 130 degrees.
  • Vertical angles are equal: the angle opposite angle BOC has the same measure as angle BOC.
  • The bisectors of two adjacent supplementary angles are perpendicular, and the converse is also true.

mcqs.q: How many basic parts does a proof have, according to Exercise 10.1?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Six. A proof has Statement, Given, Required to prove, Construction, Proof and Q.E.D. — the six parts listed in Exercise 10.1.

mcqs.q: Which part of a proof states what is given?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Given. The Given part lists what is given in the question, before stating what is required to prove.

mcqs.q: What does Q.E.D. mark at the end of a proof?
options: The proof is complete and proved
mcqs.why: The correct answer is The proof is complete and proved. Q.E.D. is the sixth part of a proof and shows the required result has been proved.

mcqs.q: In the figure of Exercise 10.2 Q1, what is the supplementary angle of angle BOC?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Angle AOC. Angle BOC and angle AOC are adjacent angles on a straight line, so they are supplementary by Theorem 1.

mcqs.q: In the same figure, what is the complementary angle of angle BOC?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Angle POC. OP is perpendicular to AB, so angle BOC and angle POC together make 90 degrees and are complementary.

mcqs.q: If m angle BOC = 50 degrees, what is its complementary angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 40 degrees. Complementary angles add to 90 degrees, so 90 degrees minus 50 degrees equals 40 degrees.

mcqs.q: If m angle BOC = 50 degrees, what is its supplementary angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 130 degrees. Supplementary angles add to 180 degrees, so 180 degrees minus 50 degrees equals 130 degrees.

mcqs.q: If 2x + 3x + 45 degrees = 180 degrees on a straight line, what is x?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 27 degrees. Adding gives 5x = 135 degrees, so x = 27 degrees, using Corollary 1 of Theorem 1 for angles on a straight line.

mcqs.q: If m angle BOC = 40 degrees at a crossing, what is m angle AOD, its vertical angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 40 degrees. Angle AOD is the vertical angle of angle BOC, and vertical angles are equal in measure.

mcqs.q: The bisectors of two adjacent supplementary angles are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Perpendicular to each other. Halving the 180 degree sum gives 90 degrees between the bisectors, so OE is perpendicular to OD.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

Theorem 3: Vertical angles are equal. When two lines cut each other, the opposite angles formed are vertical angles and have the same measure.

Theorem 1 is also used throughout: adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary and add to 180 degrees. Complementary angles add to 90 degrees.

Worked example: In the figure, if m angle BOC = 70 degrees, then angle AOD is the vertical angle of angle BOC, so m angle AOD = 70 degrees by Theorem 3. Angle AOC and angle BOC are supplementary, so m angle AOC = 180 degrees - 70 degrees = 110 degrees. Angle BOD is the vertical angle of angle AOC, so m angle BOD = 110 degrees.

Worked example: Two lines cut each other at an angle of 30 degrees. Its vertical angle is also 30 degrees by Theorem 3. The other two angles are each 180 degrees - 30 degrees = 150 degrees, supplementary by Theorem 1. Hence the other three angles are 30 degrees, 150 degrees, 150 degrees.

For figures in Question 5, pairs are sorted by their sums: complementary pairs add to 90 degrees, supplementary pairs add to 180 degrees, and vertical pairs are opposite each other. For example, in figure (i) complementary pairs are (angle c, angle d) and (angle g, angle h), supplementary pairs include (angle a, angle b), (angle e, angle f) and (angle f, angle a), and vertical pairs are (angle a, angle e) and (angle b, angle f). The same method is used for figures (ii) and (iii) in the source.

For Question 6, angles on a straight line and right angles are used together. Figure (i): x + 90 degrees + 20 degrees = 180 degrees, so x = 70 degrees. Figure (ii): y + 90 degrees + 35 degrees = 180 degrees, so y = 55 degrees, and x = 90 degrees - y = 35 degrees because x and y are complementary. Figure (iii): 90 degrees - x = 30 degrees, so x = 60 degrees, y = 90 degrees - x = 30 degrees, and z = 90 degrees - y = 60 degrees. Figure (iv): the right-angle mark lies in the x wedge, so x = 90 degrees, y = 15 degrees as a vertical angle, and z = 90 degrees.

Proof — Angle 1 Is Congruent to Angle 3

Statement: In the figure, prove that angle 1 is congruent to angle 3.

Given: Two lines cut each other, forming angles 1, 2 and 3, where angle 2 is adjacent to both angle 1 and angle 3 on straight lines.

To Prove: Angle 1 congruent to angle 3.

Construction: No extra construction is needed.

Proof:

Angle 1 + angle 2 = 180 degrees (angles on a straight line, Theorem 1).

Angle 3 + angle 2 = 180 degrees (for the same reason).

Hence angle 1 + angle 2 = angle 3 + angle 2.

Subtracting angle 2 from both sides (Axiom 5) gives angle 1 = angle 3.

That is, angle 1 congruent to angle 3.

Q.E.D.

Proof — Supplements of the Same Angle Are Equal

Statement: The supplements of the same angle are equal to each other.

Given: Angle C is the supplementary angle of both angle A and angle B.

To Prove: Angle A congruent to angle B.

Construction: No extra construction is needed.

Proof:

m angle A + m angle C = 180 degrees.

m angle B + m angle C = 180 degrees.

Hence m angle A + m angle C = m angle B + m angle C.

Subtracting m angle C from both sides (Axiom 5) gives m angle A = m angle B.

That is, angle A congruent to angle B.

Q.E.D.

Remember

  • Vertical angles are equal by Theorem 3.
  • Adjacent angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees by Theorem 1.
  • If one angle at a crossing is 70 degrees, the others are 110 degrees, 70 degrees and 110 degrees in order.
  • If one angle at a crossing is 30 degrees, the other three are 30 degrees, 150 degrees and 150 degrees.
  • Supplements of the same angle are equal — subtract the common supplement using Axiom 5.
  • Complementary pairs add to 90 degrees; supplementary pairs add to 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: According to Theorem 3, vertical angles are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Equal. Theorem 3 states that vertical angles formed when two lines cut each other are equal to each other.

mcqs.q: If m angle BOC = 70 degrees, what is m angle AOD, its vertical angle?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 70 degrees. Angle AOD is the vertical angle of angle BOC, so by Theorem 3 their measures are equal.

mcqs.q: If m angle BOC = 70 degrees, what is m angle AOC?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 110 degrees. Angle AOC and angle BOC are supplementary on a straight line, so 180 degrees minus 70 degrees equals 110 degrees.

mcqs.q: Two lines cut each other at 30 degrees. What are the other three angles?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 150, 150, 30 degrees in some order. The vertical angle is 30 degrees and each adjacent angle is 180 minus 30 equals 150 degrees.

mcqs.q: In the proof that angle 1 equals angle 3, which axiom is used when angle 2 is subtracted from both sides?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Axiom 5. After angle 1 + angle 2 = angle 3 + angle 2, subtracting angle 2 from both sides by Axiom 5 gives angle 1 = angle 3.

mcqs.q: The supplements of the same angle are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Equal to each other. If angle C supplements both angle A and angle B, subtracting m angle C gives m angle A = m angle B.

mcqs.q: In Question 6 figure (i), x + 90 degrees + 20 degrees = 180 degrees, so x equals:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 70 degrees. Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees, so x = 180 minus 90 minus 20 equals 70 degrees.

mcqs.q: In Question 6 figure (ii), if y = 55 degrees and x and y are complementary, x equals:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 35 degrees. Complementary angles add to 90 degrees, so x = 90 degrees minus 55 degrees equals 35 degrees.

mcqs.q: A pair of angles that adds to 90 degrees is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Complementary. By definition complementary angles have measures that add to 90 degrees, as used throughout Exercise 10.3.

mcqs.q: A pair of adjacent angles on a straight line adds to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 180 degrees. By Theorem 1, angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, so adjacent angles there are supplementary.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.4
lessons.notes_html:
Concept

Theorem 4 is the SAS congruence rule: if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of another triangle, the triangles are congruent. Corresponding sides and angles of congruent triangles are then equal. This exercise uses SAS again and again, together with Theorem 1 (angles on a straight line), Theorem 3 (vertical angles) and Theorem 7 about parallel lines.

Describing the main figure in Question 1 in words: two lines AB and CD cut each other at point O in the middle. Joining A to C and B to D forms two opposite triangles AOC and BOD at the crossing.

Proof — AC Congruent to BD When Two Lines Cut Each Other

Statement: AB and CD are two lines cutting each other at point O. Prove that AC is congruent to BD.

Given: AB and CD cut each other at O, with O bisecting both lines, so OA congruent to OB and OC congruent to OD.

To Prove: AC congruent to BD.

Construction: Join A to C and B to D.

Proof:

In triangle AOC and triangle BOD: OA congruent to OB and OC congruent to OD (O bisects both lines).

Angle AOC congruent to angle BOD (vertical angles, Theorem 3).

Hence triangle AOC congruent to triangle BOD (SAS, Theorem 4).

Hence AC congruent to BD (corresponding sides of congruent triangles).

Q.E.D.

Proof — Vertical Angles Are Equal

Statement: If two lines cut each other, their vertical angles are equal to each other.

Given: Two lines cut each other, forming four angles: angle 1, angle 2, angle 3, angle 4.

To Prove: Angle 1 = angle 3 and angle 2 = angle 4.

Construction: No extra construction is needed.

Proof:

Angle 1 + angle 2 = 180 degrees and angle 3 + angle 2 = 180 degrees (Theorem 1).

Hence angle 1 + angle 2 = angle 3 + angle 2.

Subtracting angle 2 gives angle 1 = angle 3 (Axiom 5).

Similarly angle 2 = angle 4.

Hence the vertical angles are equal.

Q.E.D.

Proof — All Four Angles of a Rectangle Are Equal

Statement: All four angles of a rectangle are equal to each other.

Given: ABCD is a rectangle, with angle A = 90 degrees by definition, AD parallel to BC and AB parallel to CD.

To Prove: Angle A = angle B = angle C = angle D = 90 degrees.

Construction: No extra construction is needed.

Proof:

AD parallel to BC, so angle A + angle B = 180 degrees (same-side interior angles, Theorem 1), so angle B = 90 degrees.

AB parallel to CD, so angle B + angle C = 180 degrees, so angle C = 90 degrees.

And angle C + angle D = 180 degrees, so angle D = 90 degrees.

Hence all four angles are equal (each 90 degrees).

Q.E.D.

Proof — Bisector of Vertex Angle of Isosceles Triangle Is Perpendicular to Base

Statement: In an isosceles triangle, the bisector of the vertex angle is perpendicular to the base.

Given: Triangle ABC has AB congruent to AC, and AD bisects angle A, meeting BC at D.

To Prove: AD perpendicular to BC.

Construction: Draw AD, the bisector of angle A, meeting BC at D.

Proof:

In triangle ABD and triangle ACD: AB congruent to AC (given).

Angle BAD congruent to angle CAD (AD is the bisector).

AD is common.

Hence triangle ABD congruent to triangle ACD (SAS, Theorem 4).

Hence angle ADB = angle ADC.

But angle ADB + angle ADC = 180 degrees (angles on a straight line), so each is 90 degrees.

That is, AD perpendicular to BC.

Q.E.D.

Proof — Every Point on Perpendicular Bisector Is Equidistant from Ends

Statement: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of a line is equidistant from the ends of the line.

Given: OP is the perpendicular bisector of AB, that is, OP perpendicular to AB and O is the midpoint of AB. P is any point on OP.

To Prove: AP congruent to BP.

Construction: Join P to A and P to B, forming triangles AOP and BOP.

Proof:

In triangle AOP and triangle BOP: AO congruent to BO (O is the midpoint).

Angle AOP = angle BOP = 90 degrees (OP perpendicular to AB).

OP is common.

Hence triangle AOP congruent to triangle BOP (SAS).

Hence AP congruent to BP.

Q.E.D.

Proof — Medians of Equal Sides of Isosceles Triangle Are Equal

Statement: The medians of the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are equal to each other.

Given: Triangle ABC has AB congruent to AC. BD and CE are the medians of the two equal sides; D is the midpoint of AC and E is the midpoint of AB.

To Prove: BD congruent to CE.

Construction: Draw the medians BD and CE.

Proof:

In triangle ABD and triangle ACE: AB congruent to AC (given).

Angle A is common.

AD congruent to AE (halves of equal sides: AD = (1/2) AC, AE = (1/2) AB).

Hence triangle ABD congruent to triangle ACE (SAS, Theorem 4).

Hence BD congruent to CE.

Q.E.D.

Proof — From an Exterior Point, More Than One Perpendicular Cannot Be Drawn

Statement: From an exterior point, more than one perpendicular cannot be drawn to a line.

Given: Point P is outside line l.

To Prove: Only one perpendicular can be drawn from P to l.

Construction: Suppose, for contradiction, two perpendiculars PA and PB are drawn from P to line l.

Proof:

Suppose the contrary: from an exterior point P, two perpendiculars PA and PB can be drawn to line l.

Then triangle PAB would have two right angles (angle PAB and angle PBA).

This contradicts Corollary 1 of Theorem 6 (a triangle has at most one right angle).

Hence the supposition is false, and only one perpendicular can be drawn from P to l.

Q.E.D.

Question 8 uses a figure in words: a transversal cuts two lines forming angles 1, 2, 3 and 4.
